questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int {csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t-\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 10\operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{10}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =5(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,10\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\frac{\pi }{6})⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=2{e}^{(2t+1)},$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t+1.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 2{e}^{(2t+1)}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 3{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{e}^{u}+{c}_{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3{e}^{(2t+1)}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\frac{3{e}^{(2t+1)}}{2}⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral of a vector-valued function. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{4}^{16}⟨6t-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{16}⟨6t-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{4}^{16}(6t-1)\,\text{d}t,\,{\int }_{4}^{16}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

For the first component,

$$
\int (6t-1)\,\text{d}t=3{t}^{2}-t.
$$

For the second component,

$$
\int \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t=\sqrt{t}.
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{16}⟨6t-1,\,\frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨(3{t}^{2}-t){|}_{4}^{16},\,(\sqrt{t}){|}_{4}^{16}⟩ \\  & =⟨(3\cdot {16}^{2}-16)-(3\cdot {4}^{2}-4),\,4-2⟩ \\  & =⟨(768-16)-(48-4),\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨752-44,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨708,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨708,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral of a vector-valued function. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨$
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $⟩$
questions.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t,\,{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

For the first component, let $u=3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t$, so $\text{d}u={csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

For the second component, we integrate directly:

$$
\int -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟨\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡t}{3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t},\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(3-\operatorname{cot}⁡t){|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(3)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(2),\,2\,(0-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{3}{2}),\,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨ln\,(\frac{3}{2}),\,-\sqrt{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}\,,4{e}^{-2t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t,\int 4{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨6\sqrt{t}+{c}_{1},\,-2{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨6\sqrt{1}+{c}_{1},\,-2{e}^{-2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨11,\,-2{e}^{-2}+3⟩ \\ ⟨6+{c}_{1},\,-2{e}^{-2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨11,\,-2{e}^{-2}+3⟩.\end{aligned}

Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$
